notes.meaning: Nahum writes down a weighty message from God against the mighty capital city of Nineveh. Nahum's name means 'comfort,' and his message brought hope to God's oppressed people while warning their cruel enemy of ruin. Nineveh had repented a century earlier when Jonah preached there, but its people later returned to their wicked ways.

The Lord is a jealous God who loves his people deeply and will not share his honor with idols. His anger is not an uncontrolled temper like human rage, but a pure desire to set things right. He patiently holds back his wrath until the proper time, when he will bring complete justice upon his enemies.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars view verses 2 through 8 as a partial alphabet poem that was originally a separate hymn and added later by an editor.

notes.meaning: God is patient and does not punish evil right away, but his patience comes from great power rather than weakness. He never overlooks sin or lets guilty rebels walk away without justice. Even fierce whirlwinds and storm clouds are under his control, moving like dust kicked up beneath his feet.

The Lord shows his power over creation by drying up deep seas and wide rivers with a single command. Famous regions known for rich pastures and lush trees, such as Bashan, Carmel, and Lebanon, wither when he takes away their moisture. Since even the greenest earth dries up before him, no human empire can resist his command.

High mountains shake and rugged hills melt away before the Lord. The entire world and every living creature on it tremble in his holy presence. Mountains and earth only stand firm because God's favor holds them together from moment to moment.

No human being can stand up against God's boiling anger or survive his judgment. His wrath pours out like liquid fire, splitting solid rocks into pieces. It is foolish for anyone to harden their heart against a God so great and holy.

Even in the middle of fierce warnings, the Lord reveals his goodness. He is a safe fortress where his people can run when trouble strikes, and that trouble will last only for a set time. God knows and watches over everyone who places their trust in him.

The Lord will wipe out Nineveh like an overwhelming wall of water that sweeps away every defense. Her ruins will vanish completely, and her stubborn people will be chased into thick darkness. This warning was fulfilled literally when river waters broke through the city's walls during its final siege.

Nineveh may make clever plots against the Lord, but he will bring them to a sudden stop. His blow against the city will be so complete that he will never need to strike them a second time. Believers can take comfort knowing that any enemy attacking them is ultimately fighting God himself.

The Assyrian leaders act as fierce and tangled as thorny bushes, but God will easily throw them into the fire. They are drunk with pride and luxury, which leaves them dizzy and easy to push over. Like bone-dry straw in a field, they will burn up in a moment.

A wicked leader came out of Nineveh to plot destruction against the Lord and his people. King Sennacherib and his officers mocked the true God and claimed that the Lord was powerless to rescue Jerusalem. Because Nineveh nurtured such evil plans, the city brought God's judgment down on its own head.

The Assyrians seem healthy, united, and too numerous to count, but God will mow them down like tall grass. The Lord had allowed Assyria to discipline Judah for a season, but he promises that this painful correction is now over. God's people can trust that their trials have limits set by his love.

The Lord promises to break the heavy wooden bar that Assyria placed on Judah's neck and snap their chains. Judah had lived under foreign tribute and constant terror, but God was stepping in to set them free. True freedom always comes when the Lord breaks the power of the oppressor.

The Lord announces that Nineveh's royal family will end and leave no children to carry on the king's name. God will smash the carved idols inside their temples and prepare a shameful grave for the ruler because his deeds are detestable. Those who build their lives on pride and idols will ultimately find themselves completely ruined.

A runner rushes over the mountains with wonderful news of peace and deliverance for Judah. With the cruel Assyrian army destroyed, God's people can freely travel to Jerusalem, celebrate their religious feasts, and pay their vows, which are promises made to God in times of distress. God invites his people to respond to his rescue with sincere worship and joyful thanksgiving.

differ.view: Many evangelicals see this announcement of peace as pointing forward to the good news of Jesus Christ in the gospel.
Some evangelicals believe this prophecy will be fully realized only when Christ establishes his future earthly kingdom.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars suggest this verse was written as part of a festival liturgy to celebrate the fall of Nineveh in 612 B.C.
